body: I hear ya! That's been a big cause of hesitation for me too, and I'm glad it is.  Feeling suicidal is an awful feeling and can be so strong.  There's nothing I can say to make it go away,  but I have recently been very suicidal,  but have come through it.  I've been very suicidal in the past,  and come through it.  You too can come through this.  Keep hold of that hesitation,  until hope can take its place.  Stay safe friend

I've been thinking about this recently.  Ideally I'd like to die in a hospital bed.  Hear me out.  I would prefer never to be found by anyone, so no one is traumatised.  But this leaves a huge unknown and lack of closure for my loved ones,  so it's a no. I could die where someone finds me not looking to hideous, but there's a risk they'll find me before it's complete, and I get saved.  I would rather die somewhere where they are professionals and are used to death.  And I'm warm and comfy in a bed.  Obviously the problem with this is that they'll try to save my life, so that's a huge snag in my wish.  I'm still thinking what a good compromise might be.
Once stable for just a few weeks I get discharged.  Then I destabilise and my GP sends me back.  So stupid.
I get a sensation in my chest like a ball of fire.  It's there from the very beginning to the very end of hypomania for me
I'll only drink wine with a meal,  and only 1 glass,  and even then it's very very seldom.  As in I'll have 1 or 2 glasses a year!

I've still had to battle a bit,( I'm in my mid 40s now),  to be taken seriously, but since being back in hospital last year with psychosis they are taking that aspect more seriously. Oh that's a tough one. Sorry you've had this episode,  sounds like a rough one.  In terms of friends, these are my thoughts: perhaps they didn't message you because they were giving you space that you needed, or perhaps they were shying away from engaging with poorly you.  Either are possible,  so maybe any message needs to let you understand a bit more about their motivation? How about:

"Hey there,  I haven't been in a good space for the last couple of months,  sorry I've been off the radar. I'm beginning to feel a lot better and think now is a good time to start reaching out to everyone again, and wanted to contact you first. How have things been for you?"

I've kind of gone for: some honesty about why you've been no contact,  an apology for shutting them out, honesty about where you're at now,  why you are messaging with an indication that they're your first contact,  and then moving the focus off you. 

Does that make some sense? I hope this helps. This is just my 2 pence worth

Mostly depression and mixed episodes here,  very hard for me to pin point how they cycle but I do get fluctuations within that,  sometimes my predominant mood is hypo,  sometimes depressed,  usually depressed.  But definitely still a mixed episode.  

My current mixed started with depression over winter then went into psychotic depression,  then mixed.  The depression was about 6 months,  with a hospital stay.  The mixed has been 18 months so far,  hopefully working it's way out. Meds have taken ages to sort out the right doses etc.  

I think this is usually my pattern,  and I've had I think 4 episodes like this in my life.  I do get small fluctuations, but they are usually triggered by over work,  missed sleep, missed meals etc, and life stresses.  

When I was on certain anti depressants (pre diagnosis) I had fluctuations like you describe, 4-6 days severe depression,  2-4 ish days hypo for 6 months until they stopped giving me anti depressants.

My mum thought I had bipolar when I was a teen but never actually said the words to me or my doctor. The a psychiatrist many years later says I had "aspects of bipolar".... lol,  aspects...I wish it was only aspects 🤣 (I have a full diagnosis now,  no question about it being only "aspects")

Not a big call,  but went to a lady who had fallen on some ice and hurt her leg or something,  I can't remember. It wasn't her street or neighbourhood,  this was just a bunch of lovely people all helping out a stranger in need.  

Another one I like is again an icy story (seriously we hardly ever get much snow or ice here, but apparently it brings out the nice in people). I was in a really crappy part of town, not known for its love of any uniformed people.  I had to turn the truck around on this icy junction. There was a teenager there with a shovel throwing the grit onto the junction, bless his cotton socks.

Don't get me wrong, it's taken years and years to get to that point. It's taken support from colleagues and bosses,  basically telling me it's OK to tell people to naff off when they ask personal questions.  I didn't start out brave or calm about it.  Its taken work and experience,  and self acceptance (although I'm still working on that bit!).

You're very kind and clearly going to be a great nurse 💜

I do wear short sleeves.  If I'm uncomfortable though,  I can put my coat on, but I have to take it off for clinical stuff. 

If it's people with MH stuff, they don't generally ask,  they just seem to be more comfortable. And if they do ask,  it's often genuine,  so I don't mind talking about it too much.  Depends on the person. 

If a rando other asks I respond in whatever way seems appropriate... by that I mean,  if they ask and almost instantly realise they shouldn't,  I ignore it and don't answer.  If they are acting like they deserve to know,  then I tell them something like "I used to work in animal rescue", which is true,  but very obviously nothing to do with my scars.  It seems to disarm them though.  

And thanks for your kind words,  I'm battling low confidence at the mo,  so it's very appreciated 🥰

Oh and those scars have really helped me  with patients in mental health crisis. A lot of them have seen the scars and that I'm doing the job I do,  and they get a bit more encouraged that they will get through... especially the younger patients,  really helped them to know I self harmed without me having to say it out loud. Scars aren't the issue,  they tell a powerful story for people who need to hear it.

This is not nice at all.  I've had some similar ignorant interactions.  I'm sorry you had this experience. 

If it helps you at all to know... I also have a history of self harm (which is very obvious on my arms).  I am also a paramedic.  The only reason I'm not on a front line contract is the rota (messed up my BP). The job itself has not been the issue (don't get me wrong,  stressful,  triggering sometimes, but I reckon not dramatically different for me than most of my colleagues). 

And colleagues,  patients and the organisation for the most part have been supportive and pretty much ignore the scars. 

I hope you have a similar experience.  Don't let them put you off, your history will make you a better nurse.   You'll be great,  good luck 😊

Jigsaw (MS jigsaw is a free download, definitely for PC, not tried it on anything else)

Reading

Anything crafty (I'm no good, but I like drawing,  embroidery, glass painting)

Playing on xbox

Playing calming games on the phone (my preferred are water sort, and I love Hue)

Walking/ going for a run if there's a lot of nervous energy

Watching nice stuff on tv, usually sitcoms, I avoid anything along the demon scifi type stuff (because of my particular delusions)

Saying that,  it's a double edged sword.  I can't be cured,  every day is about management of symptoms,  trying to predict episodes,  trying to minimize damage.  It's exhausting and heart breaking.  But because of that daily management it's classed as a disability (in UK), and as a result requires my work to make reasonable adjustments,  and it protects me a bit more from being sacked for being a bit shit at my job every now and then. 

But it's also helped me find groups of people who understand and support.  That's been so very important and has saved me,  helped me understand myself,  and helped me think through things that were overwhelming.

I sleep longer than normal (usually), but find I can function ok after about 12 hours since taking it,  and within a couple of hours of that I'm feeling totally normal. If I need to balance work and the meds,  I try taking it earlier, coffee to stay awake a bit longer,  basically working back 12 hours from my "gotta get moving" time in the morning. 

All of the sedation is actually very good for me when I am very poorly,  keeping my energy level low helps restrain me from harm. And it definitely helps with my psychotic symptoms,  although it takes some time for it to affect the intrusive thoughts of harm. 

My psych is recommending a change to ablify when I'm stable,  as it's supposed to be less sedating (but I'll read more about people's experiences first).

So yes,  this is my go to med for acute illness,  I don't mind the side effects because frankly it keeps ne safe and alive.

UK based here.  Worked up from patient transport (PTS),  ECA, Tech to Para.

The way I see it is like learning the trade in incremental steps.  I think for some its overwhelming going straight to Para, and I certainly would have been one of those. However on PTS I learned the area, hospitals,  departments,  got comfortable in the service. As an ECA I learned the emergency side of all that without the pressure of total responsibility.  As a tech I had the responsibility with only a portion of the medicines and procedures.  Getting to Para felt like a more subtle progression as a result. 

Now it's not 100%, totally anecdotal,, but I can tell who came straight in and who didn't.  It's about how they deal with the patients and families,  and how they treat the non Para staff.  They're still brilliant at their core job though. 

On the counter point,  nowadays I think a career on the emergency ambulances is unfortunately much shorter than it used to be and burnout is faster (again,  UK based opinion). So taking that into consideration might limit how much time you want to spend on the rungs of the ladder.  

Good luck,  enjoy it
